headings.title: Introduction to Nursing Documentation
headings.content: Nursing documentation is a written or electronic legal account of the nursing care delivered to a patient. It serves as the primary communication tool among multidisciplinary healthcare team members to ensure continuity and safety of care. Every entry made in the patient record reflects the nursing process: assessment, diagnosis, planning, implementation, and evaluation.

headings.title: Purposes and Objectives of Patient Records
headings.content: Patient records extend far beyond simple shift updates. They support clinical decision-making, provide legal protection for both the patient and the nurse, and serve as evidence in courts of law. Additionally, health institutions utilize aggregated records for quality improvement audits, nursing research, reimbursement processes, and student education.

headings.title: Legal and Ethical Guidelines in Documentation
headings.content: Patient records are strictly confidential documents protected by professional ethics and statutory laws. Nurses must respect privacy by sharing patient information only with authorized personnel directly involved in care. Legally, the golden rule applies: if care was not documented, it legally was not done. Altering records after an adverse event constitutes falsification and carries severe professional penalties.

headings.title: Characteristics of Quality Nursing Documentation
headings.content:
Good documentation must be factual, accurate, complete, current, and organized. 

- **Factual**: Based on what the nurse sees, hears, smells, or feels, avoiding vague terms like 'patient had a good day.'
- **Accurate**: Uses precise measurements, exact times, and approved medical abbreviations.
- **Complete**: Contains all essential information without leaving out critical clinical changes.
- **Current**: Entries are recorded at the time care occurs, never delayed until the end of a shift.

headings.title: Methods and Systems of Health Record Keeping
headings.content: Healthcare facilities use different charting systems to organize patient data. Traditional source-oriented records separate notes by discipline, where nurses write in one section and doctors in another. Problem-oriented medical records (POMR) focus on specific patient problems using a database, problem list, initial plan, and progress notes. Charting by exception (CBE) streamlines entries by documenting only significant deviations from established normal baselines.

headings.title: Guidelines for Effective Nursing Reporting
headings.content: Nursing reporting refers to the oral, written, or digital exchange of information between caregivers, most commonly during shift change handovers. Effective reports must be concise, relevant, and structured logically. Standardized tools like ISBAR (Introduction, Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) prevent miscommunication during patient transfers between units or shifts.

headings.title: Reporting Incidents and Unusual Occurrences
headings.content: An incident report is an administrative tool used to document any event that falls outside the normal routine of hospital operations, such as a patient fall, medication error, or needle stick injury. The primary purpose of incident reporting is quality improvement and risk management, not disciplinary action. Nurses must document the factual incident details in the report but should NEVER mention the incident report inside the patient's clinical medical record.

headings.title: Common Errors in Documentation and How to Avoid Them
headings.content: Documentation errors compromise patient safety and legal standing. Common pitfalls include charting in advance, omitting signatures, using unapproved abbreviations, and making illegible handwritten entries. When a charting error occurs on paper, the nurse must draw a single line through the mistake, write 'error,' and initial it, never erasing or using correction fluid.
